entries.topicDescription: Classic and idiomatic design patterns applied through Kotlin's language features.

tips.title: Prototype pattern via copy() for cheap, safe object cloning
tips.content:
Manually reconstructing a complex object field-by-field to create a
slightly modified variant is verbose and breaks the moment a new property
is added to the class, since every clone site needs updating too.

Kotlin's data class copy() function implements the Prototype pattern for
free — it creates a new instance with all the same properties, letting
you override only the ones that differ, and stays correct automatically as
the class evolves.
tips.codeSnippet:
data class RequestConfig(val url: String, val timeoutMs: Long, val retries: Int)

val base = RequestConfig("https://api.example.com", 30_000, 3)
val fastVariant = base.copy(timeoutMs = 5_000) // prototype-style clone with one change

tips.title: Template Method via an abstract class with default step implementations
tips.content:
Template Method defines the overall skeleton of an algorithm in a base
class while letting subclasses override specific steps, so common
sequencing logic isn't duplicated across every variant.

An abstract class with a final (non-open) orchestrating function, plus
open or abstract step functions, gives subclasses control over individual
steps without letting them change the overall order of operations.

tips.title: Adapter pattern makes an incompatible interface usable
tips.content:
When integrating a third-party SDK or legacy class whose interface doesn't
match what your code expects, changing the third-party code usually isn't
possible or safe.

An Adapter wraps the incompatible type and implements the interface your
code expects, translating calls internally — this is the same idea as a
repository implementation adapting a network SDK's API to your domain's
repository interface.

tips.title: Composite pattern treats individual items and groups uniformly
tips.content:
Modeling a tree structure (like nested UI components or a file system)
becomes awkward if code has to constantly check 'is this a single item or
a group?' before deciding how to process it.

Composite gives both leaves and groups the same interface, so calling code
can treat a single item and an entire subtree identically — a common
example is a UI component tree where a Container is itself just another
Component.

tips.title: Sealed classes are Kotlin's idiomatic State pattern
tips.content:
The classic State pattern uses subclassing plus a context that delegates to
the current state object. Kotlin's sealed class hierarchies give you this for
free, with the added benefit of exhaustive `when` checks at compile time.

Model each state as a sealed subclass, and let the compiler catch you if a
new state is added but a `when` block forgets to handle it — this is exactly
what an ApiResult sealed class does for network states like Loading,
Success, and Error.

tips.title: Chain of Responsibility with suspend function composition
tips.content:
The classic CoR pattern links handler objects, each deciding whether to
process a request or pass it along. In Kotlin, a chain of suspend
interceptors — each wrapping a `next` call — achieves the same thing without
needing a base Handler class hierarchy.

This is exactly how OkHttp/Ktor interceptor chains work internally: auth,
retry, and logging interceptors each decide to short-circuit or delegate to
the next link, composing cleanly without any of the links knowing about
each other.

tips.title: Repository interfaces as an Anti-Corruption Layer
tips.content:
In DDD terms, an Anti-Corruption Layer translates a foreign model (a REST
DTO, a third-party SDK type) into your domain's own vocabulary so upstream
changes don't ripple through your business logic.

A repository interface in the domain module, implemented in the data module
with a DTO-to-domain mapper, is a natural ACL: the domain never sees a DTO,
and a backend field rename only touches the mapper, not every call site.

tips.title: Facade pattern to simplify a multi-module subsystem
tips.content:
When a feature needs to coordinate several lower-level services — auth,
caching, analytics — exposing all of them to the caller leaks implementation
details and couples the caller to internals that may change independently.

A Facade class exposes one simple entry point that internally orchestrates
the subsystems, so callers depend on a stable, minimal surface instead of
wiring multiple collaborators themselves.

tips.title: Saga pattern for multi-step operations with compensation
tips.content:
A single distributed or multi-step operation (e.g. reserve inventory, charge
card, create shipment) can fail partway through, leaving the system in an
inconsistent state if there's no rollback strategy.

The Saga pattern defines each step alongside a compensating action, and runs
compensations in reverse order if a later step fails — this keeps the system
consistent without needing a distributed transaction coordinator.

tips.title: Proxy pattern to guard access to sensitive operations
tips.content:
A Proxy exposes the same interface as a real subject but adds a layer of
control — access checks, lazy initialization, or logging — without the
caller knowing the difference.

This is the same idea behind wrapping a DexGuard RASP ThreatEngine behind a
minimal interface: the proxy controls what's exposed and when the real,
sensitive implementation is invoked, keeping the real object's structure out
of the public API surface.

tips.title: Builder pattern replaced by named arguments and defaults
tips.content:
The classic Builder pattern exists to work around constructors with many
optional parameters in languages without named arguments. Kotlin has named
arguments and default parameter values built in, so a fluent Builder class
is usually unnecessary overhead.

Reach for a real Builder only when construction requires validation steps,
incremental accumulation (like StringBuilder), or a fluent DSL — not just to
handle optional fields.
tips.codeSnippet:
// No builder needed:
data class HttpRequestConfig(
    val url: String,
    val method: String = "GET",
    val timeoutMs: Long = 30_000,
    val retries: Int = 3
)

val config = HttpRequestConfig(url = "https://api.example.com", retries = 5)

tips.title: Strategy pattern via function types instead of interfaces
tips.content:
The Strategy pattern swaps an algorithm at runtime by depending on an
abstraction rather than a concrete implementation. In Kotlin, a function
type parameter often replaces a whole Strategy interface hierarchy.

This keeps call sites terse for simple cases, while you can still fall back
to an interface when a strategy needs multiple related methods or internal
state, which a single lambda can't express cleanly.

tips.title: Observer pattern via StateFlow/SharedFlow, not manual listeners
tips.content:
Manual Observer implementations (listener lists, callback interfaces) need
hand-written thread-safety and cleanup to avoid leaking references to
destroyed Activities or Fragments.

StateFlow and SharedFlow give you the Observer pattern with built-in
lifecycle-safe collection (via collectAsStateWithLifecycle or
repeatOnLifecycle), automatic replay of the latest value for new
subscribers, and no manual unsubscribe bookkeeping.

tips.title: Decorator pattern via Kotlin extension functions on interfaces
tips.content:
Decorator wraps an object to add behavior without modifying its class or
affecting other instances. Instead of a full wrapper-class hierarchy,
Kotlin often achieves the same effect by composing small interface
implementations that delegate to a wrapped instance via `by`.

Class delegation (`by`) lets a decorator implement an interface by
forwarding to a wrapped instance automatically, so you only override the
methods you actually want to change behavior for.

tips.title: Factory pattern with sealed classes for exhaustive object creation
tips.content:
A Factory centralizes object creation logic so callers don't need to know
concrete types. Pairing a factory function with a sealed input type lets the
compiler guarantee every case produces a result — no fallthrough `else`
branch masking a missing case.

This is especially useful for mapping DTO discriminator fields (e.g. a
"type" field from an API) to the correct domain subtype without scattering
if/else chains across the codebase.

tips.title: Visitor pattern via sealed hierarchies and exhaustive when
tips.content:
The classic Visitor pattern uses double-dispatch (accept/visit method
pairs) to add new operations over a fixed set of types without modifying
those types. In Kotlin, a sealed hierarchy plus an exhaustive `when`
achieves the same goal more simply, since the compiler already guarantees
every type is handled.

Reach for a true Visitor with accept/visit methods only when the type
hierarchy is open (not sealed) and defined outside your control — for a
sealed hierarchy you own, `when` is simpler and equally exhaustive.
tips.codeSnippet:
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val radius: Double) : Shape
data class Square(val side: Double) : Shape

fun area(shape: Shape): Double = when (shape) { // acts as the 'visit' operation
    is Circle -> Math.PI * shape.radius * shape.radius
    is Square -> shape.side * shape.side
}

tips.title: Command pattern encapsulates an action as an object for queuing or undo
tips.content:
Directly calling a method when a user taps a button loses the ability to
queue, log, delay, or undo that action later — the intent to act and the
act itself are fused together.

Wrapping an action as a Command object (or a data class with an execute
and an undo function) lets you store, replay, or reverse operations,
which is how undo/redo stacks and offline action queues are typically
implemented.

tips.title: Mediator pattern centralizes communication between components
tips.content:
When several UI components or subsystems need to react to each other's
changes directly, they end up holding references to one another, creating
a tangled web of dependencies that's hard to test or modify.

A Mediator sits between them: components notify the mediator of events,
and the mediator decides how to route those events to other components —
no component needs to know about any other directly, only about the
mediator.

tips.title: Memento pattern captures and restores an object's internal state
tips.content:
Implementing undo for a complex, mutable object by manually tracking
which fields changed is error-prone and tightly couples the undo logic to
the object's internals.

Memento has the object itself produce an opaque snapshot (often just a
data class copy of its state) that can be handed back later to restore
that exact state — Kotlin's data class copy() function makes this pattern
nearly free to implement for immutable state.

tips.title: Flyweight pattern shares immutable instances to cut memory overhead
tips.content:
Creating a new object for every occurrence of a value that's expensive to
construct but has a small set of distinct variants (icons, formatted
strings, style objects) wastes memory when many occurrences share the
same underlying value.

Flyweight caches and reuses immutable instances keyed by their
distinguishing parameters, so repeated requests for the same 'flyweight'
return the identical shared object instead of allocating a new one —
Kotlin's object declarations and simple map-based caches make this
straightforward to implement.

tips.title: Bridge pattern decouples an abstraction from its implementation
tips.content:
Subclassing an abstraction for every combination of feature and platform
(WindowsButton, MacButton, WindowsCheckbox, MacCheckbox) causes a
combinatorial explosion of classes as new dimensions are added.

Bridge splits the abstraction (Button, Checkbox) from its implementation
(RenderingEngine) by holding a reference to the implementation rather than
inheriting from it — both hierarchies can then vary independently without
multiplying subclasses.

tips.title: Null Object pattern replaces null checks with a no-op implementation
tips.content:
Returning null to represent 'no value' forces every caller to null-check
before using the result, and a forgotten check crashes at runtime.

A Null Object is a real instance of the expected type that implements
every method as a safe no-op or default value, so callers can use it
unconditionally without any null check at all — useful for optional
collaborators like an analytics tracker in tests or a disabled feature
flag's handler.

tips.title: Specification pattern composes business rules as combinable objects
tips.content:
Embedding complex filtering logic (eligibility rules, search filters)
directly inside a single large boolean function makes each individual
rule hard to test, reuse, or combine differently in another context.

A Specification wraps a single predicate as an object implementing an
'isSatisfiedBy' check, and specifications can be combined with and/or/not
operators — this lets you build complex rules by composing small, tested,
reusable pieces instead of duplicating logic.

tips.title: Custom Iterator implementation via operator fun iterator()
tips.content:
The for-in loop syntax isn't limited to built-in collections — any type
can be made iterable by implementing operator fun iterator() that returns
an Iterator, letting your own domain types participate in for-loops and
destructuring the same way a List does.

This is the Iterator pattern applied through Kotlin's operator conventions
instead of a Java-style Iterable<T> interface implementation, and works
even on types you don't control via an extension function.
